report:
### Conclusion
Scientific evidence demonstrates that routine arthroscopic surgery (joint endoscopy)—including lavage and debridement—is **not effective** for treating knee osteoarthritis.

### Evidence Summary
* **Landmark Trials:** Major randomized controlled trials (RCTs), such as those by Moseley et al. (2002) and Kirkley et al. (2008), compared knee arthroscopy directly against sham (placebo) surgery and optimized medical/physical therapy. They found no significant difference in pain relief, joint stiffness, or physical function between patients receiving arthroscopy and those receiving non-surgical care or placebo procedures (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4010873/).
* **Comparative Efficacy:** Subsequent RCTs and systematic reviews confirm that arthroscopy offers no meaningful or superior long-term advantage over physical therapy and non-surgical treatments for patients with degenerative knee osteoarthritis (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12891-024-07813-3, https://kpjmd.com/ask/is-arthroscopic-surgery-effective-knee-osteoarthritis/).
* **Clinical Guidelines:** Leading medical organizations, including the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS), advise against performing routine arthroscopy or debridement for knee osteoarthritis because the procedure exposes patients to surgical risks without proven therapeutic benefit (https://www.aetna.com/cpb/medical/data/600_699/0673.html).

Current clinical guidelines prioritize non-surgical management—such as structured physical therapy, exercise, weight management, and pharmacological pain relief—as the primary standard of care. Arthroscopy is generally restricted to clear mechanical blockages (such as a locked knee joint), rather than generalized osteoarthritis pain.
